title: One trigger matches two playbooks
when: Something happens that would start two different playbooks.
steps: The dispatcher runs neither.
It asks the authorized user which one, naming both.
never: Pick a playbook on its own.
why: Two playbooks for one event can send conflicting messages. The authorized user chooses.

title: A playbook step would cross the closed track
when: A step in a playbook asks an agent to do something the track does not allow (for example an agent other than 11 messaging a client directly).
steps: The dispatcher refuses the step.
The playbook is halted and the halt is recorded as a defect in the playbook (an integrity violation).
Nobody decides it on the spot: the playbook itself must be fixed.
never: Let a playbook step override the track, or treat it as a judgment call.
why: A playbook that asks for something forbidden is wrongly written. Fixing the playbook is the only safe answer.
you_see: The halted playbook and the integrity record naming the defect.
test: During an open house playbook, Agent 06 tries to send a client an invitation directly (only Agent 11 may message clients). Stand-in: the test sends it as Agent 06.

title: There is more work than capacity
when: Work is waiting because the system is at capacity.
steps: Work is let in by priority: alerts first, then active transaction deadlines, then client requests, then internal and marketing work, then prospecting.
Within the same priority, the older item goes first.
never: Let low-priority work jump the line.
why: When everything cannot happen at once, deadlines and people come before marketing and discovery.
you_see: Nothing to do; the record shows the order.
test: The authorized user's queue is full with 25 questions, so a withdrawal, two new listings and a prospecting lead wait. Three questions are marked done; the withdrawal goes first, then the two listings (older first), then the prospecting lead.

title: The authorized user's signed instruction conflicts with a playbook
when: A playbook says to do something and the authorized user signs a decision not to.
steps: The authorized user's signed decision wins.
The playbook ends and its after-action report records the authorized user's decision as a deviation.
never: Carry on with the playbook against the authorized user's signed decision.
why: Playbooks serve the authorized user. The signed decision stands, and the report shows where it departed from the standard.
you_see: The after-action report listing the authorized user's decision.
test: The weekly seller report playbook (P18) holds this week's report; the authorized user cancels it. Nothing is sent to the seller and the report lists the authorized user's cancellation.

title: Data is too old
when: Data a task needs is older than its freshness limit.
steps: It is regenerated fresh; stale items are left out and counted.
why: Old data in a moving market misleads.
you_see: Fresh data, with a count of what was dropped as stale.
test: A comparables request where one sale was retrieved too long ago.

title: One step fails while others run alongside it
when: Several independent steps happen together and one of them fails.
steps: The steps that do not depend on it still finish.
The failed step is flagged and held for the authorized user; anything that depends on it waits.
The work is never abandoned silently.
never: Drop the whole job, or hide the failure.
why: One broken step should not stop unrelated work, and must not go unnoticed.
you_see: A question about the failed step; the rest done.
test: A lead named "Jane Synth": filing into the client drawer fails (a space is not allowed in the folder name); capture, scoring and the CRM log still complete.

title: The same message arrives twice
when: An identical message (same ID) arrives a second time.
steps: The dispatcher processes it once.
The second arrival is answered as a duplicate and does nothing.
never: Act on the same message twice.
why: A retry that runs twice could double a message to a client or a booking.
test: The test sends one inquiry twice with the same message ID.

title: It is unclear whether a legal line is crossed
when: An agent cannot tell whether something crosses the legal line.
steps: It treats it as crossed.
It stops and raises a legal-line alert for the authorized user.
never: Give the benefit of the doubt on a legal question.
why: A false alarm costs a minute; a missed legal problem can cost a license.
test: A closing statement arrives and Agent 08 has no list of expected senders, so it cannot tell if the sender is legitimate: it is quarantined and escalated, and nothing moves the closing.

title: No decision exists for the situation
when: Something happens that no tuple covers.
steps: The agent stops.
It asks the authorized user and waits.
why: A missing decision is a gap in the design, to be decided by the authorized user, not filled in on the fly.
you_see: A question saying no rule covers this and the item is held.
test: A social media mention reading "lol", labeled noise, which no rule covers.

title: Keeping the agents on their rules over long runs
when: An agent has been working for a long time, or reaches a major step.
steps: At every major step (for example taking in a new listing, going live), the agents are handed the conduct rules again.
If many turns pass without that, a backstop hands them over anyway.
never: Run for long stretches on fading instructions.
why: Software agents can drift from their instructions over long runs. Re-reading the rules keeps behavior consistent.
you_see: Nothing; the record shows each re-reading.
test: A new listing goes live; the record shows the conduct rules re-read at its phase gates.

title: Acting when not everything is known yet
when: The path looks clear but not everything is confirmed.
steps: Agents go ahead only with steps that can be undone.
Anything that cannot be undone or that a client or other party will see waits for the authorized user's full, signed authority.
never: Take an irreversible or public step on partial information.
why: Reversible steps keep work moving; irreversible ones need certainty.
you_see: The photographer booking and the listing ad waiting for the authorized user's release.
test: A new listing: the photographer booking and the marketing publish are both held for the authorized user's signed release.

title: Two jobs need the same agent at once
when: Two running playbooks need the same agent at the same moment.
steps: The higher-priority job goes ahead.
The other waits on a "siding" and resumes when the agent is free.
Neither job is cancelled.
never: Abort a job because of a clash.
why: Clashes are normal on a busy day; waiting the authorized user's turn is safe, aborting loses work.
you_see: Nothing; the record shows the hold and the resume.
test: A withdrawal and two new listings all need Agent 05; the withdrawal goes first and the two listings wait on the siding, then resume in arrival order.

title: A task would need a route that does not exist
when: An agent tries to send something on a path the track does not declare.
steps: The dispatcher refuses it before delivery.
never: Treat a missing route as permission.
why: An undeclared path is a sign something is wrong, not an opportunity.
test: Agent 06 asks Agent 14 for a client's record (no such route). Stand-in: the test sends it as Agent 06.

title: A situation comes up that no rule covers, during a playbook
when: Inside a playbook, an agent meets something no tuple covers.
steps: The agent holds it and asks the authorized user.
The playbook's after-action report proposes a new tuple for it, for the authorized user to approve.
why: Each gap found becomes a new decision. That is how the system gets more complete over time, with the authorized user deciding each addition.
you_see: A question saying no rule covers it; a proposed tuple in the after-action report.
test: During an open house, a client asks "Can you run the ad on Instagram too?"; Agent 12 has no rule for it. The open house report proposes one.
